mechanism_fit: M13 cross-file competition, built as R9 describes. The trigger (TarArchiveEntryTest::testHeaderBytesRoundTrip) works directly on TarArchiveEntry. It sets fields, calls entry.writeEntryHeader(header) by name, rebuilds the entry with new TarArchiveEntry(header) (which calls parseTarHeader), and reads getModTime(). So the competitors are the long writeEntryHeader and parseTarHeader methods plus setModTime(long) and getModTime, all in TarArchiveEntry.java, the class the test names and the easiest place to look. The gold is TarUtils.getLongOctalBytes, in a different file, one call below writeEntryHeader. The gold and every decoy run under the trigger (G6). The failure (modTime 1262304000000 ms comes back as 188562176000 ms, while name, mode, ids, user/group names and size round-trip) fits any of them: a seconds/millis conversion, the writer's field layout, the reader's field layout, the octal parser, or the octal formatter. Other correct competitors in the gold's own file: TarUtils.getOctalBytes and TarUtils.parseOctal.
ownership_reason:
The trigger round-trips a TarArchiveEntry through writeEntryHeader and the TarArchiveEntry(byte[]) constructor (parseTarHeader). Every field survives except the modification time, which comes back as 188562176 s instead of 1262304000 s. In octal, 1262304000 is 11317235400 (11 digits) and 188562176 is 1317235400: the same value with its leading digit dropped. So the 12-byte MODTIMELEN field received only 10 digits.

The reader side is pinned correct. TarTestCase.testTarUnarchiveEntryAttributes passes on the variant: it reads GNU tar's bla.tar, whose 12-byte modTime field holds the 11 digits 10716545626, and parseTarHeader/parseOctal/getModTime return 1195035542000 ms. No reader edit can restore a digit that is not in the header bytes.

The writer's layout is pinned correct too. writeEntryHeader passes the TarConstants lengths at the same offsets parseTarHeader reads, and every other trigger field round-trips. getOctalBytes is pinned by TarTestCase.testTarHeaderChecksumAndTypeFlag, which also passes on the variant. getOctalBytes fills exactly `length` bytes: digits, then a space, then a trailing NUL. getCheckSumOctalBytes relies on that layout when it rewrites the last two checksum bytes, so getOctalBytes cannot be widened without corrupting the checksum or the type flag after it.

getLongOctalBytes is the helper that gives the 12-byte size and modTime fields length-1 digit positions. It allocates temp = new byte[length + 1] so that getOctalBytes' trailing NUL falls outside the `length` bytes copied into the header. The variant formats only `length` bytes into that temp. The copied field is therefore 10 digits, a space and a NUL, and the extra temp byte is never used. The same helper also writes the size field (a second caller), which loses its leading digit for any size of 8^10 bytes or more. So the defect is in the shared helper, not in the modTime-specific code of TarArchiveEntry.

The minimal repair restores getOctalBytes(value, temp, 0, length + 1) in TarUtils.getLongOctalBytes.
construction_notes:
Project: Compress (Defects4J Compress-1f). The fault is one token in TarUtils.getLongOctalBytes: getOctalBytes(value, temp, 0, length + 1) becomes getOctalBytes(value, temp, 0, length). There are no context edits; every decoy is byte-identical to pristine (G11).

Screening on a /private/tmp copy:
- Variant: full suite 0 failures out of 73 tests (the fault is undetected). Only the new trigger fails.
- Correct configuration: everything passes.

Tests added:
- Trigger testHeaderBytesRoundTrip in TarArchiveEntryTest (JUnit 3 style; neutral name).
- Ownership test testTarUnarchiveEntryAttributes in TarTestCase: reads bla.tar's first entry and checks name, mode 0644, size 610 and modTime 1195035542000 ms.
- Ownership test testTarHeaderChecksumAndTypeFlag in TarTestCase: recomputes the header checksum and checks the LF_DIR type flag and isDirectory after a round trip. It needs imports of TarConstants and TarUtils.

The checksum/type-flag test was needed. Without it, three one-line widenings of getOctalBytes pass both the trigger and the existing suite, because this Compress version never verifies tar checksums:
- idx = length - 1 changed to idx = length;
- dropping the --idx after the NUL;
- dropping the --idx after the space.
They are now declared as compensating edits: each passes the trigger but fails the ownership test, so none absorbs the fault.

The other declared compensating edits all leave the trigger failing:
- writeEntryHeader uses getOctalBytes for modTime;
- parseTarHeader reads MODTIMELEN - 1 bytes;
- setModTime(long) rounds;
- getModTime multiplies with a long cast.

concerns:
1. An undeclared, contrived one-line writeEntryHeader edit would also make the trigger and the full suite pass: offset = TarUtils.getLongOctalBytes(modTime, outbuf, offset, MODTIMELEN + 1) - 1. It writes 13 bytes into the 12-byte field, and the spilled byte is then overwritten by the checksum-space loop. It is a workaround rather than a repair: it leaves the size field (the second caller of the gold) broken for sizes of 8^10 bytes or more. G9 does not cover it.
2. Both ownership tests are new tests added by this construction, not pre-existing ones. The checksum/type-flag test exists specifically to pin getOctalBytes.
3. The variant line can be spotted locally (temp is allocated with length + 1 but formatted with length). Once an agent opens TarUtils the gold is probably easy to find, so the mechanism depends on the agent stopping at TarArchiveEntry.
4. The trigger also round-trips a small size (4096) through the same gold, and that assertion passes. An agent may use this to infer that the failure depends on the value's magnitude.
5. The javadoc of getLongOctalBytes ("Parse an octal long integer from a header buffer") is pristine but misleading, since the method formats rather than parses. It was left unchanged.
